4.9 What the Comparison Shows

  • All four logistic regressions beat both bars for all eligible donors. Their gains over prior-year giving run from 5.9 to 6.7 points, each with a paired 95% interval above zero, and each also clears the former major or $500 rule. Erin’s untuned model puts 82.1% of converters on the list (75.3% to 88.2%), 6.7 points above the prior-year ranking (2.2 to 11.4) and 5.5 points above the former major or $500 rule (1.8 to 9.7).
  • None of them measurably beats the bar for never-major donors. Their point gains run from -0.3 to 4.8 points, and every interval includes zero. All four are well ahead of the former major or $500 rule for these donors, since for them that rule is only the $500 threshold.
  • R1 keeps Erin’s untuned model. No challenger clears the test against it. The closest is Kate’s: the same recall for all eligible donors, and 3.4 points more for never-major donors (-2.0 to 10.2), about 2 more of the 59 never-major converters. Kate’s model also had the highest inner average precision for every test cohort. With more converters to test on, her additions may prove their worth, so hers is the variant to retest first on PBS Utah’s own records. Under the rule we wrote, the simpler model stays.
  • Tuning did not settle on one penalty. The tuned candidates chose quite different penalty strengths from one test cohort to the next (see the table above). With 55 to 145 training converters, the inner folds cannot pin the penalty down, which fits with the untuned default doing as well as any tuned setting.
  • R2 keeps the use list. With every input, Erin’s model finds 79.1% of converters for all eligible donors (-3.0 points against the use list, -8.1 to 1.9) and 62.7% for never-major donors (1.7 points, -7.8 to 8.5). Solicitation, Passport viewing, and recency add nothing measurable once giving history is known, as every individual notebook found, and neither do the engineered features. This answers the revised business problem’s question of whether engagement and viewing add anything: in this release, they add nothing measurable to the ranking.
  • The tree models fall below the logistic regressions. The random forest finds 79.1%, histogram gradient boosting 74.6%, and LightGBM 72.4%. For never-major donors, LightGBM and histogram gradient boosting are measurably worse than the prior-year ranking itself (-8.8 and -8.8 points). This matches our individual notebooks and supports setting them aside (decision D9).
  • Run time. Erin’s model fits all three test cohorts in 0.6 seconds in total, with no tuning. Each tuned logistic candidate spent 5.2 to 6.5 minutes on inner cross-validation, and each tree model 1.7 to 3.7 minutes. The whole comparison took about 26 minutes of fitting the first time; later renders read the saved results.

The selected model is therefore Erin’s untuned L2 logistic regression on the giving-history use list, trained on FY2021 onward. The next section looks at how it performs beyond the main test: in each cohort, in the checks R3 reports, and in how well its probabilities are calibrated.

5 Model Performance

5.1 The Selected Model

The selected model is Erin’s untuned L2 logistic regression on the giving-history use list, trained on cohorts from FY2021 onward. This section reports how it performs in more settings than the main comparison:

  • Training cohorts and test cohorts. In-sample and out-of-sample performance side by side.
  • Each test cohort and other list sizes. Results by year, and for lists shorter and longer than 1,000.
  • The R3 checks. The FY2025 cohort, held back from every comparison and scored once. The cohorts before the cultivation program. The donors untouched by simulated contact. The FY2014 training window. The model without contact flags. None of these can change the model (R3).
  • Calibration (R7). Whether the probabilities are about right, and the range of converters staff should expect from a list.

Two fits of the selected model are used here. The check model trains on FY2021 to FY2024 and scores the FY2025 cohort. The final model trains on FY2021 to FY2025, every cohort whose 12 month outcome is known, and is the one that scores the FY2026 donors in the last section (decision D5).

FINAL_SPEC = {**CANDIDATES[SELECTED][0], "features": FINAL_FEATURES}
FINAL_GRID = CANDIDATES[SELECTED][1]
FINAL_RUN = all_run if r2_replaces else runs[SELECTED]   # the selected model's rolling-test predictions

def fit_final(train_end, spec=FINAL_SPEC, grid=FINAL_GRID, target="y_12m", data=None):
    """Fit a model on its training cohorts from train_start through train_end, tuning first when it has a grid."""
    data = frame if data is None else data
    train = data.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(spec["train_start"], train_end) & pl.col(target).is_not_null())
    chosen, tune_seconds = spec, 0.0
    if grid:
        start = perf_counter()
        tbl = tune(spec, grid, train, target)
        tune_seconds = perf_counter() - start
        best = tbl.sort("average_precision", descending=True)["params"][0]
        chosen = {**spec, "model": clone(spec["model"]).set_params(**grid[[str(g) for g in grid].index(best)])}
    X, cols = design(train, chosen["features"])
    est = build(chosen, cols)
    start = perf_counter()
    est.fit(X, train[target].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy())
    return {"estimator": est, "columns": cols, "spec": chosen, "train_end": train_end, "training_rows": train.height,
            "training_converters": int(train[target].sum()), "tune_seconds": tune_seconds,
            "fit_seconds": perf_counter() - start}

def score_with(fitted, df):
    # probabilities for df's donors with the contact flags off, and the time it took
    X, _ = design(scoring_view(df), fitted["spec"]["features"])
    start = perf_counter()
    p = predict_score(fitted["estimator"], X)
    return df.select("constituent_id", "t").with_columns(score=pl.Series(p)), perf_counter() - start

check_model = fit_final(2024)   # scores the FY2025 cohort once
final_model = fit_final(2025)   # every cohort with a known 12 month outcome

# a refit through FY t-1 reproduces the rolling test's scores for cohort t, so the two code paths agree
for T in TEST_COHORTS:
    refit, _ = score_with(fit_final(T - 1), scored.filter(pl.col("t") == T))
    rolled = FINAL_RUN[0].filter(pl.col("t") == T)
    assert refit["constituent_id"].equals(rolled["constituent_id"])
    assert np.allclose(refit["score"].to_numpy(), rolled["score"].to_numpy(), rtol=0, atol=1e-12)

5.2 Training and Test Performance

In-sample is the check model scored on the FY2021 to FY2024 cohorts it was trained on. Out-of-sample is the rolling test, where each cohort was scored by a model trained only on earlier cohorts. Both are scored with the contact flags off.

PERF_SCORES = {"model": "model_score", "prior-year giving": "prior_total", "former major or $500": "rule_former_or_500"}

def mean_average_precision(df, col):
    # average precision within each cohort, averaged over cohorts
    return float(np.mean([average_precision_score(d["y"].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy(), d[col].to_numpy()) for d in df.partition_by("t")]))

def performance(setting, df, pred):
    """Recall at 1,000 for the model and the bars on df's cohorts, with paired gains for all eligible and never-major donors."""
    d = df.join(pred.rename({"score": "model_score"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    assert d["model_score"].null_count() == 0
    b_all, b_never = bootstrap(d, PERF_SCORES), bootstrap(d.filter(~pl.col("former_major")), PERF_SCORES)
    g_all, g_never = paired(b_all, "model", "prior-year giving"), paired(b_never, "model", "prior-year giving")
    g_rule = paired(b_all, "model", "former major or $500")
    lo, hi = np.quantile(b_all["draws"]["model"][:, 0], [0.025, 0.975])
    years = sorted(d["t"].unique().to_list())
    return {"setting": setting, "cohorts": f"FY{years[0]} to FY{years[-1]}" if len(years) > 1 else f"FY{years[0]}",
            "converters": int(d["y"].sum()), "recall": b_all["point"]["model"][0], "recall_low": lo, "recall_high": hi,
            "precision": b_all["point"]["model"][1], "prior_year_recall": b_all["point"]["prior-year giving"][0],
            "gain": 100 * g_all["gain"], "gain_low": 100 * g_all["low"], "gain_high": 100 * g_all["high"],
            "gain_vs_rule": 100 * g_rule["gain"], "gain_vs_rule_low": 100 * g_rule["low"], "gain_vs_rule_high": 100 * g_rule["high"],
            "never_major_converters": int(d.filter(~pl.col("former_major"))["y"].sum()),
            "never_major_recall": b_never["point"]["model"][0], "never_major_prior_year": b_never["point"]["prior-year giving"][0],
            "never_major_gain": 100 * g_never["gain"], "never_major_gain_low": 100 * g_never["low"],
            "never_major_gain_high": 100 * g_never["high"],
            "average_precision": mean_average_precision(d, "model_score"),
            "prior_year_average_precision": mean_average_precision(d, "prior_total")}

in_sample = scored.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(FINAL_SPEC["train_start"], 2024))
in_sample_pred, _ = score_with(check_model, in_sample)
perf = pl.DataFrame([performance("training cohorts (in-sample)", in_sample, in_sample_pred),
                     performance("rolling test (out-of-sample)", test, FINAL_RUN[0])])
pf = {r["setting"].split(" (")[0]: r for r in perf.iter_rows(named=True)}
PERF_COLS = ["setting", "cohorts", "converters", "recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "prior_year_recall", "gain", "gain_low",
             "gain_high", "never_major_recall", "never_major_gain", "average_precision", "prior_year_average_precision"]
PERF_FIXED = {"gain": 1, "gain_low": 1, "gain_high": 1, "never_major_gain": 1, "average_precision": 3, "prior_year_average_precision": 3}
show(perf.select(PERF_COLS), pct_cols=["recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "prior_year_recall", "never_major_recall"],
     fixed=PERF_FIXED,
     caption="Selected model in-sample and out-of-sample: recall at 1,000, paired gain over prior-year giving in points, and average precision")
model_test = test.join(FINAL_RUN[0].rename({"score": "model_score"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
model_never = model_test.filter(~pl.col("former_major"))
by_year = recall_by_cohort(model_test, {"model": "model_score", "prior-year giving": "prior_total"}).join(
    recall_by_cohort(model_never, {"never_major_model": "model_score", "never_major_prior_year": "prior_total"})
    .rename({"converters": "never_major_converters"}), on="cohort")
by_year = by_year.with_columns(gain=(pl.col("model") - pl.col("prior-year giving")) * 100,
                               never_major_gain=(pl.col("never_major_model") - pl.col("never_major_prior_year")) * 100)
show(by_year, pct_cols=["model", "prior-year giving", "never_major_model", "never_major_prior_year"],
     fixed={"gain": 1, "never_major_gain": 1},
     caption="Recall at 1,000 in each test cohort for the selected model and prior-year giving, with the gain in points")
ins, oos = pf["training cohorts"], pf["rolling test"]
assert abs(ins["recall"] - oos["recall"]) < 0.02 and ins["average_precision"] > oos["average_precision"]
assert (by_year["gain"] > 0).all()
never_short = {r["cohort"]: r["never_major_gain"] / 100 * r["never_major_converters"] for r in by_year.iter_rows(named=True)}
"training and test claims hold"
'training and test claims hold'
  • Little sign of overfitting. On the cohorts it was trained on, the model holds 82.5% of converters, against 82.1% out of sample. Average precision drops only from 0.252 to 0.229. With a small set of inputs and the default penalty, the model has little room to memorize the training donors, and the out-of-sample gain over prior-year giving (6.7 points) is close to the in-sample gain (7.5).
  • Ahead in every test cohort. The gain over prior-year giving is 12.0, 0.8, 5.2 points in FY2022, FY2023, and FY2024. For never-major donors the yearly gains are 2.0, -1.9, 4.9 points. With 16 to 22 never-major converters a year, the FY2023 shortfall is less than one converter.
  • Average precision more than doubles. Across the test cohorts the model’s average precision is 0.229, against 0.083 for prior-year giving. The model orders donors within the list much better than the prior-year ranking does, which matters most for the shorter lists below.

5.3 Recall at Other List Sizes

A list of 1,000 is about the cultivation program’s capacity, but PBS Utah could work a shorter list more closely or hand a longer one to annual-giving staff.

size_rows = []
for k in (250, 500, 1000, 2000):

        d_ = paired(b, "model", "prior-year giving")
        size_rows.append({"list_size": k, "group": g, "model_recall": b["point"]["model"][0],
                          "prior_year_recall": b["point"]["prior-year giving"][0], "model_precision": b["point"]["model"][1],
                          "gain": 100 * d_["gain"], "gain_low": 100 * d_["low"], "gain_high": 100 * d_["high"]})
sizes = pl.DataFrame(size_rows)

show(sizes, pct_cols=["model_recall", "prior_year_recall", "model_precision"], fixed={"gain": 1, "gain_low": 1, "gain_high": 1},
     caption="Recall by list size on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts, with the paired gain over prior-year giving in points")
def recall_at(df, col, k):
    # pooled recall at k over df's cohorts, ties at the cutoff split evenly
    hits = sum((share_on_list(w, gid, k) * w * y).sum() for _, y, w, gid in ranked(df, col))
    return hits / float((df["y"] * df["w"]).sum())

    for g, df in (("All eligible donors", model_test), ("Never-major donors", model_never))
    for name, col in (("Selected model", "model_score"), ("Prior-year giving", "prior_total"))
]).to_pandas()

5.4 Checks Reported Under R3

The checks below were set before any result (R3). They describe how far the main result travels, and none of them can change the model.

  • FY2025. The check model scores the FY2025 cohort once. Its outcomes fall in FY2026, the year of the donor influx the group EDA found.
  • Before the program. The FY2018 to FY2021 cohorts, each scored by a model trained on FY2014 through the year before, since FY2021 onward leaves nothing to train on. No donor in these cohorts was selected or contacted, so this is the cleanest test of ranking donors by their own giving history.
  • Without simulated contact. The no-contact pool and the donors not selected for cultivation, from the Benchmarks section.
  • Two variants. The FY2014 training window (decision D7) and the model refit without the contact flags (decision D11), each on the rolling test.

'R3 claims hold'
  • FY2025: no gain in the influx year. Scored once, the check model holds 69.1% of the 81 FY2025 converters, the same as prior-year giving (0.0 points, -7.0 to 8.4). It still beats the former major or $500 rule by 4.3 points (0.6 to 10.0). The FY2025 cohort converted at 0.25%, against 0.11% to 0.17% in the test cohorts, the FY2026 influx the group EDA described. When conversion jumps like this, the model’s edge over prior-year giving can disappear. This is the main risk to report with the model.
  • Before the program: a gain for never-major donors too. On the FY2018 to FY2021 cohorts, where no donor was selected or contacted, the model holds 86.8% of 197 converters against 82.5% (4.3 points, 1.7 to 6.1). For never-major donors the gain is 4.3 points (1.0 to 7.8), the only setting where it is measurable. These cohorts train on FY2014 onward, with more converters to learn from, and simulated contact plays no part. That makes this the cleanest evidence that giving history alone adds something.
  • Without simulated contact. On the no-contact pool the model holds 80.1% against 72.2% for prior-year giving, with an interval too wide to call (-2.0 to 19.7). Among donors officers did not select there are only 25 converters, and the model holds 36.0% against 41.5% (-18.4 to 4.6), too few to say anything.
  • Officer selection, as an illustration. On the no-contact pool the model’s top 1,000 holds 9.4 points more converters than the donors officers chose (3.9 to 21.3), and 12.9 points more among never-major donors (3.0 to 28.2). The cultivation tables were invented, so this only shows how the comparison would work once PBS Utah records contacts (decision D13).
  • The two variants change little. Training on FY2014 onward gives 84.3%, 2.2 points more than the selected model (-0.8 to 4.8), and 3.4 points more for never-major donors (0.0 to 8.7). Without the contact flags the ranking moves by 0.7 points. Under R3 neither changes the model, but the longer window is worth retesting once PBS Utah’s own records are in hand.

5.5 Calibration

Staff see each donor’s probability of becoming a major donor next year, so the probabilities should be about right, not just the order. R7 compares the predicted and observed number of converters, pooled over the test cohorts. If the ratio falls outside 0.8 to 1.25, the probabilities get a one-parameter intercept correction for each test cohort, estimated on that cohort’s most recent training cohort scored with the contact flags off. The correction changes the probabilities staff see but never the order of the list. Inside that range the probabilities are reported as they are.

from scipy.optimize import brentq

def calibration_by_band(df, score_col):
    # predicted and observed conversion by position in the ranking, pooled over cohorts
    bands = [(1, 100), (101, 250), (251, 500), (501, 1000), (1001, 2000), (2001, 5000), (5001, None)]
    ranked_df = df.with_columns(position=pl.col(score_col).rank("ordinal", descending=True).over("t"))
    rows = []
    for lo, hi in bands:
        sel_ = ranked_df.filter(pl.col("position") >= lo) if hi is None else ranked_df.filter(pl.col("position").is_between(lo, hi))
        rows.append({"ranks": f"{lo:,} and below" if hi is None else f"{lo:,} to {hi:,}", "donor_years": sel_.height,
                     "converters": int(sel_["y"].sum()), "predicted_converters": float(sel_[score_col].sum()),
                     "mean_predicted": sel_[score_col].mean(), "observed_rate": sel_["y"].mean()})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

def intercept_shift(p, observed):
    # the shift on the log-odds scale that makes the probabilities add up to the observed converters
    logit = np.log(p / (1 - p))
    return brentq(lambda d: (1 / (1 + np.exp(-(logit + d)))).sum() - observed, -10, 10)

def shifted(p, d):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(np.log(p / (1 - p)) + d)))

pooled_ratio = float(model_test["model_score"].sum() / model_test["y"].sum())
NEEDS_RECALIBRATION = not (0.8 <= pooled_ratio <= 1.25)   # R7

# the correction each test cohort would get, from its latest training cohort (computed either way, applied only under R7)
shifts = {}
for T in TEST_COHORTS:
    prev = scored.filter(pl.col("t") == T - 1)
    p_prev, _ = score_with(fit_final(T - 1), prev)
    shifts[T] = intercept_shift(p_prev["score"].to_numpy(), float(prev["y"].sum()))
if NEEDS_RECALIBRATION:
    model_test = model_test.with_columns(model_score=pl.struct("model_score", "t").map_elements(
        lambda r: float(shifted(r["model_score"], shifts[r["t"]])), return_dtype=pl.Float64))
calibrated_ratio = float(model_test["model_score"].sum() / model_test["y"].sum())
cal_ratio_by_year = {t: float(d["model_score"].sum() / d["y"].sum()) for (t,), d in model_test.group_by("t")}
fy25_df = fy25.join(fy25_pred.rename({"score": "model_score"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
fy25_ratio = float(fy25_df["model_score"].sum() / fy25_df["y"].sum())
cal_bands = calibration_by_band(model_test, "model_score")
show(cal_bands, pct_cols=["mean_predicted", "observed_rate"], pct_digits=2, fixed={"predicted_converters": 1},
     caption="Calibration on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts: predicted and observed next-year converters by position in the ranking")
cal_plot = cal_bands.with_columns(ranks=pl.col("ranks").cast(pl.Enum(cal_bands["ranks"].to_list()))).to_pandas()
lim = (1e-4, 0.5)
(
    ggplot(cal_plot, aes("mean_predicted", "observed_rate"))
    + geom_abline(intercept=0, slope=1, color="#8b8b84", linetype="dashed")
    + geom_point(color="#2a78d6", size=3)
    + geom_text(aes(label="ranks"), nudge_y=0.15, size=8, color="#52514e")
    + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda xs: [f"{100 * x:g}%" for x in xs], limits=lim)
    + scale_y_log10(labels=lambda ys: [f"{100 * y:g}%" for y in ys], limits=lim)
    + labs(x="Average predicted probability", y="Observed conversion rate",
           title="Predicted and observed next-year conversion, by position in the ranking",
           subtitle="FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts; points on the dashed line are calibrated (log scales)")
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 4.5))
)

R7 also asks that staff always see a range of expected converters rather than a single number. The range comes from the probabilities on the list: if each donor converts with their predicted probability, independently, the number of converters among the top 1,000 varies from year to year by chance alone. The table compares that range with what happened in each test cohort.

def converter_range(p, draws=10000, seed=SEED):
    # 95% range of the converter count when each donor converts with probability p, independently
    counts = (np.random.default_rng(seed).random((draws, len(p))) < p).sum(axis=1)
    return float(p.sum()), *np.quantile(counts, [0.025, 0.975])

range_rows = []
for t in TEST_COHORTS:
    top = model_test.filter(pl.col("t") == t).sort("model_score", descending=True).head(K)
    expected, lo, hi = converter_range(top["model_score"].to_numpy())
    range_rows.append({"cohort": t, "expected_converters": expected, "range_low": lo, "range_high": hi,
                       "observed_converters": int(top["y"].sum())})
ranges = pl.DataFrame(range_rows).with_columns(inside=pl.col("observed_converters").is_between(pl.col("range_low"), pl.col("range_high")))
show(ranges, fixed={"expected_converters": 1, "range_low": 0, "range_high": 0},
     caption="Converters among each test cohort's top 1,000: expected from the probabilities, a 95% range, and observed")
# predicted and observed converters by cohort and contact status, the FY2025 check included
cal_cols = ["t", "contacted", "model_score", "y"]
cal_year = (
    pl.concat([model_test.select(cal_cols), fy25_df.select(cal_cols)])
    .with_columns(donors=pl.when(pl.col("contacted")).then(pl.lit("contacted")).otherwise(pl.lit("not contacted")))
    .group_by("t", "donors").agg(donor_years=pl.len(), predicted_converters=pl.col("model_score").sum(),
                                 observed_converters=pl.col("y").sum())
)
cal_year = pl.concat([
    cal_year,
    cal_year.group_by("t").agg(donors=pl.lit("all"), donor_years=pl.col("donor_years").sum(),
                               predicted_converters=pl.col("predicted_converters").sum(),
                               observed_converters=pl.col("observed_converters").sum()),
], how="diagonal_relaxed").with_columns(ratio=pl.col("predicted_converters") / pl.col("observed_converters")).sort("t", "donors")
cy = {(r["t"], r["donors"]): r for r in cal_year.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(cal_year.rename({"t": "cohort"}), fixed={"predicted_converters": 1, "ratio": 2},
     caption="Predicted and observed converters by cohort and contact status, FY2022 to FY2025 (scored with contact flags off)")
assert not NEEDS_RECALIBRATION
contacted_ratios = [cy[(t, "contacted")]["ratio"] for t in (*TEST_COHORTS, 2025)]
assert all(a > b for a, b in zip(contacted_ratios, contacted_ratios[1:]))           # contacted donors fall further behind each year
assert all(cy[(t, "not contacted")]["ratio"] > 1 for t in TEST_COHORTS) and cy[(2025, "not contacted")]["ratio"] < 1
rg = {r["cohort"]: r for r in ranges.iter_rows(named=True)}
assert rg[2022]["inside"] and rg[2023]["inside"] and not rg[2024]["inside"]
top_bands = cal_bands.head(4)   # ranks 1 to 1,000
top_pred, top_obs = top_bands["predicted_converters"].sum(), top_bands["converters"].sum()
rest_pred, rest_obs = cal_bands.tail(3)["predicted_converters"].sum(), cal_bands.tail(3)["converters"].sum()
assert cal_bands["ranks"][3] == "501 to 1,000" and top_obs > top_pred and rest_obs < rest_pred
"calibration claims hold"
'calibration claims hold'
  • R7 keeps the probabilities as they are. Pooled over the test cohorts, the model predicts 0.86 converters for every one observed, inside the 0.8 to 1.25 range, so no correction is applied. By position in the ranking, the top 1,000 donors each year were predicted to produce 86 converters over the three cohorts and produced 110, while below rank 1,000 the model predicted 29 and 24 converted. The list holds more converters than its probabilities say, and the rest of the cohort fewer.
  • The pooled ratio hides two errors that offset. By cohort the ratio is 1.08, 1.00, 0.47 for FY2022 to FY2024 and 0.23 for FY2025. Contacted donors are predicted further below what they did each year (0.74, 0.55, 0.23, 0.14). Donors are scored with the contact flags off, so their probabilities leave out the effect of contact, and in this release simulated contact steered more and more conversion toward selected donors from FY2023 on. Donors who were not contacted are predicted above what they did in FY2022 to FY2024, most likely because part of the contacted donors’ extra conversion was credited to the giving patterns officers select on. In FY2025 even donors who were not contacted converted at 2.4 times the predicted rate, the influx again.
  • Ranges for the list. The 95% range of converters expected in the top 1,000 held what happened in FY2022 (43 converters, range 34 to 56) and FY2023 (28, range 19 to 37), but not FY2024, when 39 converted against a range of 7 to 21.

The probabilities are best read as what to expect from donors without officer contact, in a year like the ones the model was trained on. That is a fair basis for ordering the list. As a forecast of how many donors will convert, it ran low in the years when simulated contact or the influx pushed conversion up. The range shown with the FY2026 list in the last section has to carry this caveat.

5.6 Run Time

runtime = pl.DataFrame([
    {"step": "fit the check model (FY2021 to FY2024)", "rows": check_model["training_rows"], "seconds": check_model["fit_seconds"]},
    {"step": "fit the final model (FY2021 to FY2025)", "rows": final_model["training_rows"], "seconds": final_model["fit_seconds"]},
    {"step": "score the FY2025 cohort", "rows": fy25.height, "seconds": fy25_seconds},
    {"step": "rolling test, three fits", "rows": int(FINAL_RUN[1]["training_rows"].sum()), "seconds": float(FINAL_RUN[1]["fit_seconds"].sum())},
])
show(runtime, digits=3, caption="Run time of the selected model")

The selected model is fast at every step. The final model fits 160,919 donor-years in 0.6 seconds and scores a full cohort of 32,886 donors in 0.01 seconds. Refitting it each year after the June 30 cutoff costs PBS Utah almost nothing; most of the time in this notebook goes to the bootstrap intervals and to tuning the challengers, not to the model itself.

6 What the Model Finds

The model beats the prior-year ranking by about seven points for all eligible donors. This section explains where that gain comes from, so staff can see why the list differs from a sort by last year’s giving. It looks at the top 1,000 lists on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts in three ways, then at what the final model weighs:

  • Who is on the list. Erin’s list composition: how many former-major and never-major converters each list catches, and how many of its places go to each group.
  • Who the model finds that prior-year giving misses. Kate’s breakdown of converters by prior-year giving band, split by which list found them.
  • What drives the score. The final model’s coefficients.

Lapsed donors, who gave in one of the two years before FY t but not in FY t, are outside every list by decision D3; the last subsection reports how many of them convert.

6.1 Who Is on the List

def with_list_share(df, col, name, k=K):
    # each row's share of a place on its cohort's top-k list by col, ties at the cutoff split evenly
    parts = []
    for d in df.partition_by("t"):
        gid = (d[col].rank("dense", descending=True) - 1).cast(pl.Int64).to_numpy()
        parts.append(d.with_columns(pl.Series(name, share_on_list(d["w"].to_numpy(), gid, k))))
    return pl.concat(parts)

lists = with_list_share(with_list_share(model_test, "model_score", "on_model"), "prior_total", "on_prior")
assert abs(lists.group_by("t").agg(pl.col("on_model").sum(), pl.col("on_prior").sum())
           .select(pl.col("on_model", "on_prior") - K).to_numpy()).max() < 1e-9   # every list has exactly 1,000 places

def composition(df, label):
    conv_ = df.filter(pl.col("y") == 1)
    return {"donors": label, "list_places_model": df["on_model"].sum() / len(TEST_COHORTS),
            "list_places_prior_year": df["on_prior"].sum() / len(TEST_COHORTS), "converters": conv_.height,
            "found_by_model": conv_["on_model"].sum(), "found_by_prior_year": conv_["on_prior"].sum()}

comp = pl.DataFrame([composition(lists.filter(pl.col("former_major")), "former major"),
                     composition(lists.filter(~pl.col("former_major")), "never major"),
                     composition(lists, "all eligible")])
cp = {r["donors"]: r for r in comp.iter_rows(named=True)}
assert abs(cp["all eligible"]["found_by_model"] / cp["all eligible"]["converters"] - sel_all["recall"]) < 1e-9
show(comp, fixed={"list_places_model": 0, "list_places_prior_year": 0, "found_by_model": 1, "found_by_prior_year": 1},
     caption="Composition of the top 1,000 lists on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts: average places per year and converters found over the three cohorts")
fm, nm = cp["former major"], cp["never major"]
assert fm["found_by_model"] == fm["converters"] > fm["found_by_prior_year"] and fm["list_places_model"] > 1.5 * fm["list_places_prior_year"]
assert abs(nm["found_by_model"] - nm["found_by_prior_year"]) < 1
gain_former = fm["found_by_model"] - fm["found_by_prior_year"]
gain_never = nm["found_by_model"] - nm["found_by_prior_year"]
assert gain_former > 5 * gain_never
"composition claims hold"
'composition claims hold'
  • The gain comes from former major donors. The model catches 75 of the 75 former-major converters (every one of them) over the three test cohorts, against 66.7 for prior-year giving, a difference of 8.3 converters. Among never-major converters the two lists find 35.0 and 34.4, almost the same. Erin’s notebook found the same split.
  • It does this by giving former majors more places. The model gives former major donors about 170 of the 1,000 places each year, against 89 on the prior-year list. A former major who gave less than usual in FY t falls down a sort by last year’s giving, but the model still ranks them near the top.

This is the most useful thing to tell staff about the list: it is a sort by last year’s giving that pulls former major donors back up. For donors who have never been major, it does about as well as the sort it replaces, which matches the never-major results in the last two sections.

6.2 Who the Model Finds That Prior-Year Giving Misses

BAND_EDGES = [(0, 100, "under $100"), (100, 250, "$100 to $249"), (250, 600, "$250 to $599"), (600, 1200, "$600 to $1,199")]
band_expr = pl.when(pl.col("prior_total") < 100).then(pl.lit(BAND_EDGES[0][2]))
for lo, hi, label in BAND_EDGES[1:]:
    band_expr = band_expr.when(pl.col("prior_total").is_between(lo, hi, closed="left")).then(pl.lit(label))
lists = lists.with_columns(band=band_expr.cast(pl.Enum([b[2] for b in BAND_EDGES])),
                           both=pl.min_horizontal("on_model", "on_prior"),
                           model_only=(pl.col("on_model") - pl.col("on_prior")).clip(0, None),
                           prior_year_only=(pl.col("on_prior") - pl.col("on_model")).clip(0, None))
lists = lists.with_columns(neither=1 - pl.col("both") - pl.col("model_only") - pl.col("prior_year_only"))
band_table = (
    lists.group_by("band").agg(
        list_places_model=pl.col("on_model").sum() / len(TEST_COHORTS), list_places_prior_year=pl.col("on_prior").sum() / len(TEST_COHORTS),
        converters=(pl.col("y") == 1).sum(),
        **{c: (pl.col(c) * pl.col("y")).sum() for c in ("both", "model_only", "prior_year_only", "neither")})
    .sort("band")
)
bt = {r["band"]: r for r in band_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
model_only_total, prior_only_total = band_table["model_only"].sum(), band_table["prior_year_only"].sum()
assert abs((model_only_total - prior_only_total) / cp["all eligible"]["converters"] - gain_all[first]["gain"]) < 1e-9
show(band_table, fixed={c: 1 for c in ("both", "model_only", "prior_year_only", "neither")} | {"list_places_model": 0, "list_places_prior_year": 0},
     caption="Converters by FY t giving band and which top 1,000 list found them, FY2022 to FY2024; list places are averages per year")
def profile(weight, label):
    # weighted averages of a few use-list fields over the converters a list found alone
    c = lists.filter(pl.col("y") == 1).with_columns(wt=weight)
    tot = c["wt"].sum()
    avg = lambda e: float((c.select(e.cast(pl.Float64).fill_null(0) * pl.col("wt")).to_series().sum()) / tot)
    return {"converters": label, "count": tot, "former_major": avg(pl.col("former_major")),
            "average_prior_year_giving": avg(pl.col("prior_total")), "average_years_given_last_five": avg(pl.col("years_last5")),
            "soft_credit_before": avg(pl.col("soft_before").fill_null(False)), "sustainer": avg(pl.col("sustainer")),
            "average_largest_gift_share": avg(pl.col("largest_gift_share"))}

disc = pl.DataFrame([profile(pl.col("model_only"), "found only by the model"),
                     profile(pl.col("prior_year_only"), "found only by prior-year giving"),
                     profile(pl.col("both"), "found by both")])
dp = {r["converters"]: r for r in disc.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(disc, pct_cols=["former_major", "soft_credit_before", "sustainer"],
     fixed={"count": 1, "average_prior_year_giving": 0, "average_years_given_last_five": 1, "average_largest_gift_share": 2},
     caption="Profile of the converters each list found, FY2022 to FY2024 (weighted by each converter's share of a list place)")
mid = bt["$250 to $599"]
assert mid["model_only"] == max(r["model_only"] for r in bt.values())
assert bt["$600 to $1,199"]["both"] == bt["$600 to $1,199"]["converters"]
low_conv = bt["under $100"]["converters"] + bt["$100 to $249"]["converters"]
low_found = bt["under $100"]["model_only"] + bt["$100 to $249"]["model_only"]

assert mo["former_major"] > po["former_major"] and po["sustainer"] > mo["sustainer"]

assert top_band["on_prior"].sum() / top_band.height > 0.95 and top_band["on_model"].sum() / top_band.height > 0.95

tie_sizes, tie_amounts = [], []
for d in lists.partition_by("t"):
    cut = d.sort("prior_total", descending=True)["prior_total"][K - 1]
    tie_amounts.append(cut)
    tie_sizes.append(d.filter(pl.col("prior_total") == cut).height)

"band claims hold"
'band claims hold'
  • Every converter who gave $600 or more in FY t is on both lists. All 90 of them. Both lists give a place to nearly every donor in that band, so it cannot separate the two rankings.
  • The two lists differ in the $250 to $599 band. Here the model finds 12.0 converters the prior-year list misses and misses 4.0 that it finds. The prior-year list’s cutoff falls inside this band: in each test cohort the 1,000th place lands on a gift amount ($250, $250, $250) shared by 1,516, 1,431, 1,512 donors, who split the last places evenly. The model ranks those donors by the rest of their history instead.
  • Converters who gave under $250 in FY t are mostly out of reach. There were 17 of them, and the model found 1, even though it gives about 54 places a year to donors in these bands, 86% of them to former majors. Converting from under $250 to $1,200 or more in one year is rare and hard to see coming.

Who the model finds alone is just as telling. Of the 13.0 converters only the model found, 64% were former major donors. They had given in 4.6 of the last five years on average, and their largest gift was 76% of their FY t giving. Of the 4.0 that only the prior-year list found, none was a former major, 83% were sustainers, and they had given in 3.5 of the last five years. The model trades sustainers who reached the $250 to $599 range through monthly payments for donors with a past major year and one larger gift. Kate’s notebook found extra converters among $100 to $249 donors with a past major year or a long record. On the group population, the same kind of donor shows up one band higher.

6.3 What Drives the Score

The coefficients below come from the final model, trained on FY2021 to FY2025. Every input is standardized before fitting, so each coefficient is the change in the log-odds of converting for a one standard deviation increase, holding the other inputs fixed. Three inputs are left out of the chart. The contact flags are used in training only and are switched off for every donor scored. Age has no planted relationship with conversion in this release, so it stays in the model as a tested input but is not presented as a driver (decision D10). The third, an indicator for the FY2021 cohort, is explained below the chart.

pipe = final_model["estimator"]
imputer, scaler, lr = pipe[0], pipe[1], pipe[-1]
cols = final_model["columns"]
names = list(cols) + [f"{cols[i]} (missing)" for i in imputer.indicator_.features_]
assert len(names) == lr.coef_.shape[1]

def describe(name):
    base = name.split(" (missing)")[0].split("_Female")[0].split("_Male")[0].split("_Unknown")[0]
    group, _, text = FEATURES.get(base, ("", "", ""))
    return group, text + (" is missing" if name.endswith("(missing)") else "")

drivers = pl.DataFrame({"input": names, "coefficient": lr.coef_[0]}).with_columns(
    odds_ratio_per_sd=pl.col("coefficient").exp(),
    group=pl.col("input").map_elements(lambda s: describe(s)[0], return_dtype=pl.String),
    meaning=pl.col("input").map_elements(lambda s: describe(s)[1], return_dtype=pl.String),
    shown=~pl.col("input").is_in(["contacted", "held_out", "age_at_t", "soft_before (missing)"]),
).sort(pl.col("coefficient").abs(), descending=True)
dv = {r["input"]: r for r in drivers.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(drivers.select("input", "group", "meaning", "coefficient", "odds_ratio_per_sd"), digits=2,
     caption="Final model coefficients per standard deviation of each input, largest first")
dplot = drivers.filter(pl.col("shown")).with_columns(
    direction=pl.when(pl.col("coefficient").abs() < 0.02).then(pl.lit("near zero"))
    .when(pl.col("coefficient") > 0).then(pl.lit("raises the score")).otherwise(pl.lit("lowers the score"))).to_pandas()
DRIVER_LABELS = {
    "prior_total": "FY t giving", "largest_gift_share": "Largest gift's share of FY t giving", "years_last5": "Years given, last five",
    "monthly_amount": "Monthly sustaining amount", "former_major": "Former major donor", "gender_Unknown": "Gender unknown",
    "gender_Female": "Gender female", "gender_Male": "Gender male", "years_since_first_gift": "Years since first gift",
    "legacy_years": "Years with a legacy gift", "soft_before": "Soft credit before FY t", "change_from_last_year": "Change from last year",
    "two_years_before": "Giving in FY t-2 and t-1", "sustainer": "Sustainer", "monthly_amount (missing)": "No monthly amount (not a sustainer)",
}
assert set(dplot["input"]) <= set(DRIVER_LABELS)
dplot["label"] = dplot["input"].map(DRIVER_LABELS)
dplot["label"] = pd.Categorical(dplot["label"], categories=list(dplot.sort_values("coefficient")["label"]), ordered=True)
(
    ggplot(dplot, aes("coefficient", "label"))
    + geom_vline(xintercept=0, color="#8b8b84")
    + geom_segment(aes(x=0, xend="coefficient", y="label", yend="label"), color="#c9c8c3", size=1)
    + geom_point(aes(color="direction"), size=3)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"raises the score": "#2a78d6", "lowers the score": "#52514e", "near zero": "#c9c8c3"},
                         breaks=["raises the score", "lowers the score", "near zero"])
    + labs(x="Change in log-odds per standard deviation", y="", color="",
           title="What the final model (FY2021 to FY2025) weighs", subtitle="Contact flags, age, and the FY2021 indicator not shown")
    + theme(legend_position="top", figure_size=(8, 5))
)
era = dv["soft_before (missing)"]
assert drivers.filter(pl.col("shown"))["input"][0] == "prior_total"
assert dv["largest_gift_share"]["coefficient"] > 0 and dv["years_last5"]["coefficient"] > 0 and dv["former_major"]["coefficient"] > 0
assert dv["monthly_amount"]["coefficient"] < 0
assert max(abs(dv[f]["coefficient"]) for f in ("change_from_last_year", "two_years_before")) < 0.05
soft_missing_years = sorted(frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2025) & pl.col("soft_before").is_null())["t"].unique().to_list())
assert soft_missing_years == [2021]
"driver claims hold"
'driver claims hold'
  • FY t giving leads. One standard deviation more giving in FY t multiplies the odds of converting by 1.82, more than any other input.
  • The shape of a donor’s giving comes next. A larger share of FY t giving in one gift (odds ratio 1.49 per standard deviation) and more years with a gift in the last five (1.35) both raise the score. A larger monthly sustaining amount lowers it (0.76), holding FY t giving fixed. Of two donors who each gave $500, the model rates the one who gave it in a single gift above the one who reached it through monthly payments.
  • Former major status. Its own coefficient is modest (1.15), because a past major year also shows up in the largest gift share and the years given. Together these inputs lift former majors in the ranking, as the composition table shows.
  • What adds little. The change from last year and the giving two years before have coefficients near zero once FY t giving is in the model. This fits the 3-year total doing no better than prior-year giving in the Benchmarks section.
  • One coefficient describes the data, not donors. The indicator for a missing “soft credit before FY t” is large (1.69), but soft credits before FY t are missing only for the FY2021 cohort, since they were not recorded before the Unite system. The indicator absorbs whatever sets that cohort apart from the later training cohorts. It is zero for every donor scored from FY2022 on, so it cannot move anyone on a list, and it is left out of the chart.

The coefficients show what the model leans on, not why donors convert. Several inputs measure related things, so the weight can shift between them from one training window to the next, and staff should read the chart as a description of the score rather than a list of causes.

6.4 Lapsed Donors

seg = (cohorts.filter((pl.col("window") == 1) & pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2025))
       .group_by("t", "segment").agg(donors=pl.len(), converters=pl.col("converted").sum()).sort("t", "segment"))
seg_wide = seg.pivot(on="segment", index="t", values=["donors", "converters"]).with_columns(
    lapsed_rate=pl.col("converters_lapsed") / pl.col("donors_lapsed"), active_rate=pl.col("converters_active") / pl.col("donors_active"),
    lapsed_share_of_converters=pl.col("converters_lapsed") / (pl.col("converters_lapsed") + pl.col("converters_active")))
lapsed_conv = int(seg_wide["converters_lapsed"].sum())
lapsed_share = lapsed_conv / int(seg_wide["converters_lapsed"].sum() + seg_wide["converters_active"].sum())
show(seg_wide.rename({"t": "cohort"}), pct_cols=["lapsed_rate", "active_rate", "lapsed_share_of_converters"], pct_digits=2,
     caption="Lapsed and active donors at each snapshot, FY2021 to FY2025: donors, next-year converters, and conversion rates")
assert (seg_wide["lapsed_rate"] < seg_wide["active_rate"]).all() and lapsed_share < 0.05
rate_ratio = float(seg_wide["active_rate"].mean() / seg_wide["lapsed_rate"].mean())
"lapsed claims hold"
'lapsed claims hold'

Lapsed donors are about 14,134 people a year, but only 9 of them became major donors the next year across the FY2021 to FY2025 snapshots, 3.2% of all next-year converters. Active donors convert about 13 times as often. Leaving them out of the main list (decision D3) costs very few converters. A lapsed-only list, as Kate built, is an optional view for reactivation campaigns, not a source of major donors.

7 Longer Windows and Giving Tier

7.1 Becoming a Major Donor Within 3 or 5 Years

The revised business problem asks for donors likely to become major donors within three to five years, for a long-term nurture list. A strictly time-based test of a longer outcome needs training cohorts whose outcome windows had closed by the test cohort’s prediction date. For the 3 year outcome, test cohort T can train only on cohorts up to T-3, and for the 5 year outcome up to T-5. That pushes training back into the legacy-system years, so these models train on cohorts from FY1999 onward and rely on giving history (decision D15). The engagement fields were not recorded then, and the contact flags are off for every pre-program cohort. One input of the 12 month model is left out: soft credits before FY t, which were not recorded before FY2021 and are missing for every training row in these test windows. A check in the code below confirms that dropping it leaves the test scores unchanged, and the Giving Tier subsection shows why keeping it would distort scores for recent donors. We report them as projections: they rank donors by the same giving history the 12 month model uses, over a longer horizon.

Test design for the longer outcomes
Outcome Test cohorts Checked once (report only) Training cohorts for the first test
Within 3 years FY2021 and FY2022 (outcomes through FY2025) FY2023 (its window reaches FY2026) FY1999 to FY2018
Within 5 years FY2016 to FY2020 (outcomes through FY2025) FY2021 (its window reaches FY2026) FY1999 to FY2011

Under R4 the selected model’s family is the reported model: Erin’s untuned L2 logistic regression on the use list. An explainable boosting machine, with its default settings and no tuning, replaces it only if it passes the R1 test against it. Both are compared with the prior-year ranking and the former major or $500 rule on the same resamples.

from interpret.glassbox import ExplainableBoostingClassifier

LONG_START = 1999
LONG = {
    "within 3 years": {"target": "y_3yr", "window": 3, "test": [2021, 2022], "check": 2023},
    "within 5 years": {"target": "y_5yr", "window": 5, "test": [2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020], "check": 2021},
}
EBM = "explainable boosting machine"
# soft credits before FY t were not recorded before FY2021, so models trained from FY1999 leave them out
LONG_FEATURES = [f for f in FINAL_FEATURES if f != "soft_before"]
LONG_SPECS = {
    SELECTED: {**FINAL_SPEC, "features": LONG_FEATURES, "train_start": LONG_START},
    # trees handle gaps natively; a feature with no observed values in a training window is dropped first.
    # Two workers keep memory within a 16 GB laptop; each bag is seeded from random_state, so results do not depend on it
    EBM: candidate(EBM, ExplainableBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED, n_jobs=2), features=LONG_FEATURES, scaled=False,
                   drop_empty=True, train_start=LONG_START),
}
import gc
gc.collect()   # free memory left over from earlier fits before the long ones
long_runs = {
    (o, m): cached_nested({**spec, "name": f"{m}, {o}"}, None, target=cfg["target"], window=cfg["window"], test_cohorts=cfg["test"])
    for o, cfg in LONG.items() for m, spec in LONG_SPECS.items()
}

# the same runs with soft credits before FY t kept: the input is missing in every training window of these tests,
# so leaving it out cannot change the scores
for o, cfg in LONG.items():
    for m in LONG_SPECS:
        train_rows = frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(LONG_START, max(cfg["test"]) - cfg["window"]) & pl.col(cfg["target"]).is_not_null())
        assert train_rows["soft_before"].null_count() == train_rows.height
# (the boosting machine drops a column with no observed values before fitting, so for it the two versions are the same
# matrix by construction; the logistic regression, which imputes and scales the column, is refit to show it)
kept_soft = {
    (o, SELECTED): cached_nested({**LONG_SPECS[SELECTED], "features": FINAL_FEATURES, "name": f"{SELECTED}, {o}"}, None,
                                 target=cfg["target"], window=cfg["window"], test_cohorts=cfg["test"])
    for o, cfg in LONG.items()
}
long_input_diff = max(
    float(np.abs(long_runs[k][0].join(kept_soft[k][0], on=["constituent_id", "t"]).select(pl.col("score") - pl.col("score_right"))
                 .to_numpy()).max())
    for k in kept_soft
)
assert long_input_diff < 1e-6
LONG_SCORES = {"prior-year giving": "prior_total", "former major or $500": "rule_former_or_500"}

def long_frame(cfg, cohorts):
    # donor-years in the given cohorts with the longer outcome as y
    return scored.filter(pl.col("t").is_in(cohorts)).with_columns(y=pl.col(cfg["target"]), w=pl.lit(1.0))

long_rows, long_boots = [], {}
for o, cfg in LONG.items():
    df = long_frame(cfg, cfg["test"])
    for m in LONG_SPECS:
        df = df.join(long_runs[(o, m)][0].rename({"score": m}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    assert df.select(pl.col(list(LONG_SPECS)).null_count()).sum_horizontal().item() == 0
    scores = {**LONG_SCORES, **{m: m for m in LONG_SPECS}}
    for g, d in (("all eligible", df), ("never major", df.filter(~pl.col("former_major")))):
        b = long_boots[(o, g)] = bootstrap(d, scores)
        for r in summarize(b, "ranking").iter_rows(named=True):
            gain = paired(b, r["ranking"], "prior-year giving") if r["ranking"] != "prior-year giving" else None
            long_rows.append({"outcome": o, "group": g, "cohorts": f"FY{min(cfg['test'])} to FY{max(cfg['test'])}",
                              "converters": int(d["y"].sum()), "ranking": r["ranking"], "recall": r["recall"],
                              "recall_low": r["recall_low"], "recall_high": r["recall_high"],
                              "gain": None if gain is None else 100 * gain["gain"],
                              "gain_low": None if gain is None else 100 * gain["low"],
                              "gain_high": None if gain is None else 100 * gain["high"]})
long_table = pl.DataFrame(long_rows)
lt = {(r["outcome"], r["group"], r["ranking"]): r for r in long_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(long_table, pct_cols=["recall", "recall_low", "recall_high"], fixed={"gain": 1, "gain_low": 1, "gain_high": 1},
     caption="Recall at 1,000 for the longer outcomes, with the paired gain over prior-year giving in points")
# R4: the boosting machine replaces the selected family only under the R1 test
r4_rows, LONG_SELECTED = [], {}
for o in LONG:
    res, replaces = r1_compare({g: long_boots[(o, g)] for g in ("all eligible", "never major")}, EBM, SELECTED)
    LONG_SELECTED[o] = EBM if replaces else SELECTED
    r4_rows.append({"outcome": o, **{f"{k}_{g.split()[0]}": 100 * res[g][k] for g in res for k in ("gain", "low", "high")},
                    "replaces": replaces, "reported_model": LONG_SELECTED[o]})
r4_table = pl.DataFrame(r4_rows)
show(r4_table, fixed={c: 1 for c in r4_table.columns if c.split("_")[0] in ("gain", "low", "high")},
     caption="R4: the explainable boosting machine's paired gain over the selected family, in points of recall at 1,000")
# the labeled check cohorts, scored once by the reported model for each outcome (report only)
check_rows = []
for o, cfg in LONG.items():
    m = LONG_SELECTED[o]
    run = cached_nested({**LONG_SPECS[m], "name": f"{m}, {o}, check"}, None, target=cfg["target"], window=cfg["window"],
                        test_cohorts=[cfg["check"]])
    p = performance(f"{o}, FY{cfg['check']} check", long_frame(cfg, [cfg["check"]]), run[0])
    check_rows.append({"check": p["setting"], **{c: p[c] for c in R3_COLS[1:]}})
long_checks = pl.DataFrame(check_rows)
lc = {r["check"]: r for r in long_checks.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(long_checks, pct_cols=["recall", "prior_year_recall", "never_major_recall"],
     fixed={c: 1 for c in R3_COLS if "gain" in c},
     caption="Labeled checks for the longer outcomes, scored once: recall at 1,000 and the paired gain over prior-year giving in points")
long_timing = pl.concat([r[1] for r in long_runs.values()]).group_by("model").agg(
    test_cohorts=pl.len(), training_rows=pl.col("training_rows").sum(), fit_seconds=pl.col("fit_seconds").sum(),
    predict_seconds=pl.col("predict_seconds").sum()).sort("model")

"longer outcome claims hold"
'longer outcome claims hold'
  • Within 3 years. The selected family holds 68.2% of the 223 converters in its top 1,000 against 58.8% for prior-year giving, a gain of 9.4 points (4.8 to 13.7). It clears the former major or $500 rule (6.4 points, 3.0 to 10.0).
  • Within 5 years. It holds 62.0% of 708 converters against 58.4%, a smaller gain of 3.6 points (0.8 to 6.2), and it clears the former major or $500 rule (11.9 points). The further out the outcome, the closer the model comes to last year’s giving.
  • Never-major donors. For both windows the gain is not measurable: 2.8 points within 3 years (-3.0 to 8.4) and -0.5 within 5 (-3.3 to 2.4). This is the same pattern as the 12 month model, where the composition table traced the gain to former major donors.
  • R4 keeps the selected family. The explainable boosting machine is -0.9 and -0.4 points from it for all eligible donors, and neither difference is measurable in either group. It also took 7 to 9 minutes to fit, against 2 to 3 seconds for the logistic regression.
  • The labeled checks agree. Scored once, the FY2023 cohort’s 3 year outcome shows a gain of 10.1 points (4.3 to 16.4), and the FY2021 cohort’s 5 year outcome 6.0 points (2.2 to 11.1). Both windows run into FY2026, so the influx that erased the 12 month gain in FY2025 did not erase the gain over these longer windows.

For the long-term nurture list, these results support ranking by the 3 to 5 year score, with a caveat staff should hear. The score beats a sort by last year’s giving for all eligible donors, but for donors who have never been major it does about as well as that sort, not better. Which of the two windows ranks the nurture list is settled with the FY2026 lists in the last section.

7.2 Giving Tier

For donors who do convert, the business problem asks for the tier they are likely to reach: $1,200 to $1,999, $2,000 to $4,999, or $5,000 and up. The tier is measured in the conversion year, FY t+1. Under the household rule, a couple that reaches $1,200 only together is measured on its combined giving. The revised business problem says predicted tiers will be checked against the tier each donor reached, exact or within one (decision D16). With three tiers, “within one” misses only when a $1,200 converter is predicted at $5,000 and up or the reverse, so it is close to automatic and is reported for completeness.

Two approaches are compared on the FY2022 to FY2024 test converters, each trained on converters from FY1999 through the year before the test cohort. FY2021 onward alone holds too few converters to learn three tiers.

  • Most-common-tier rule. Predict the tier most common among earlier converters.
  • Multinomial logistic regression. The selected family fit to the three tiers: untuned L2 with the 12 month model’s preprocessing and inputs, except soft credits before FY t (explained below).

Under R5 the rule stands unless the regression’s gain in exact accuracy has a paired 95% interval above zero. Kate’s notebook found that the only split with some signal is whether a converter reaches $2,000. So we also score her two-level indicator, $2,000 and up or not, as a labeled weak signal for the dashboard (decision D16).

TIER_NAMES = ["$1,200", "$2,000", "$5,000+"]
TIER_START = 1999

    "constituent_id", t=pl.col("fy") - 1,
    conversion_total=pl.when(pl.col("major_combined_only")).then(pl.col("total") + pl.col("spouse_total")).otherwise(pl.col("total")),
)

    frame.filter(pl.col("y_12m"))
    .join(conversion_giving, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    .with_columns(tier=pl.col("conversion_total").cut([2000, 5000], labels=TIER_NAMES, left_closed=True).cast(pl.Enum(TIER_NAMES)))
    .with_columns(tier_code=pl.col("tier").to_physical().cast(pl.Int64))
)
assert converters["conversion_total"].null_count() == 0 and (converters["conversion_total"] >= 1200).all()
tier_counts = (
    converters.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(TIER_START, 2024))
    .with_columns(converters_in=pl.when(pl.col("t") < 2022).then(pl.lit("FY1999 to FY2021 (earliest training)"))
                  .otherwise(pl.lit("FY2022 to FY2024 (test)")))
    .group_by("converters_in", "tier").len().pivot(on="tier", index="converters_in", values="len")
    .select("converters_in", *TIER_NAMES).sort("converters_in")
)
show(tier_counts, caption="Tier reached in the conversion year by 12 month converters")
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

def modal_rule(train, test):
    return np.full(test.height, int(train["tier_code"].mode().sort()[0]))

def multinomial(train, test, features=LONG_FEATURES):
    spec = {**FINAL_SPEC, "features": features, "model": LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)}
    X, cols = design(train, spec["features"])
    est = build(spec, cols).fit(X, train["tier_code"].to_numpy())
    X_test, _ = design(scoring_view(test), spec["features"])
    proba = est.predict_proba(X_test)
    return est.classes_[proba.argmax(axis=1)], proba

def two_level(train, test):
    # Kate's indicator: probability that a converter reaches $2,000 or more
    spec = {**FINAL_SPEC, "features": LONG_FEATURES, "model": LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)}
    X, cols = design(train, spec["features"])
    est = build(spec, cols).fit(X, (train["tier_code"] >= 1).cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy())
    X_test, _ = design(scoring_view(test), spec["features"])
    return est.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

tier_parts, era_rows = [], []
for T in TEST_COHORTS:
    train = converters.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(TIER_START, T - 1))
    test_c = converters.filter(pl.col("t") == T)
    pred, proba = multinomial(train, test_c)
    pred_kept, proba_kept = multinomial(train, test_c, FINAL_FEATURES)   # with soft credits before FY t, for comparison
    era_rows.append({"cohort": T, "training_converters_with_soft_credit_recorded": float(train["soft_before"].is_not_null().mean()),
                     "predicted_5000_share_kept": float(proba_kept[:, 2].mean()), "predicted_5000_share_dropped": float(proba[:, 2].mean()),
                     "exact_accuracy_kept": float((pred_kept == test_c["tier_code"].to_numpy()).mean()),
                     "exact_accuracy_dropped": float((pred == test_c["tier_code"].to_numpy()).mean()),
                     "observed_5000_share": float((test_c["tier_code"] == 2).mean())})
    tier_parts.append(test_c.select("constituent_id", "couple_id", "t", "tier_code", "former_major").with_columns(
        modal=pl.Series(modal_rule(train, test_c)), multinomial=pl.Series(pred).cast(pl.Int64),
        **{f"p_{name}": pl.Series(proba[:, i]) for i, name in enumerate(TIER_NAMES)},
        p_2000_or_more=pl.Series(two_level(train, test_c)), training_converters=pl.lit(train.height)))
tier_preds = pl.concat(tier_parts)
assert tier_preds.height == int(test["y"].sum())
era_check = pl.DataFrame(era_rows)
show(era_check, pct_cols=[c for c in era_check.columns if c != "cohort"],
     caption="Tier model with and without soft credits before FY t: share of training converters with the input recorded, average predicted $5,000+ share, and exact accuracy")
def tier_bootstrap(df, cols, reps=REPS, seed=SEED):
    # exact accuracy for each prediction column, and the two-level AUC, on couple-clustered resamples (paired)
    couples = df["couple_id"].unique().sort()
    idx = couples.search_sorted(df["couple_id"]).to_numpy()
    hits = {c: (df[c] == df["tier_code"]).cast(pl.Float64).to_numpy() for c in cols}
    high, p_high = (df["tier_code"] >= 1).cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy(), df["p_2000_or_more"].to_numpy()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    draws = {c: np.empty(reps) for c in [*cols, "auc"]}
    for r in range(reps):
        mult = np.bincount(rng.integers(0, len(couples), len(couples)), minlength=len(couples))[idx]
        for c in cols:
            draws[c][r] = (hits[c] * mult).sum() / mult.sum()
        draws["auc"][r] = roc_auc_score(high, p_high, sample_weight=mult) if 0 < (high * mult).sum() < mult.sum() else np.nan
    return {**{c: hits[c].mean() for c in cols}, "auc": roc_auc_score(high, p_high)}, draws

tier_point, tier_draws = tier_bootstrap(tier_preds, ["modal", "multinomial"])
tier_diff = tier_draws["multinomial"] - tier_draws["modal"]
tier_rows = []
for a, label in (("modal", "most-common-tier rule"), ("multinomial", "multinomial logistic regression")):
    tier_rows.append({"approach": label, "exact_accuracy": tier_point[a],
                      "accuracy_low": float(np.quantile(tier_draws[a], 0.025)), "accuracy_high": float(np.quantile(tier_draws[a], 0.975)),
                      "within_one_tier": float(((tier_preds[a] - tier_preds["tier_code"]).abs() <= 1).mean()),
                      "predicted_2000_or_more": float((tier_preds[a] >= 1).mean())})
tier_table = pl.DataFrame(tier_rows)
tt = {r["approach"]: r for r in tier_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
tier_gain = {"gain": 100 * (tier_point["multinomial"] - tier_point["modal"]),
             "low": 100 * float(np.quantile(tier_diff, 0.025)), "high": 100 * float(np.quantile(tier_diff, 0.975))}
TIER_CHOICE = "multinomial logistic regression" if tier_gain["low"] > 0 else "most-common-tier rule"   # R5
auc_low, auc_high = np.nanquantile(tier_draws["auc"], [0.025, 0.975])
show(tier_table, pct_cols=["exact_accuracy", "accuracy_low", "accuracy_high", "within_one_tier", "predicted_2000_or_more"],
     caption="Tier predictions for the FY2022 to FY2024 test converters")
# the expected mix: observed shares among converters, and the multinomial model's average predicted shares
tier_mix = pl.DataFrame([
    {"tier": name,
     "share_of_earlier_converters": float((converters.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(TIER_START, 2021))["tier"] == name).mean()),
     "share_of_test_converters": float((tier_preds["tier_code"] == i).mean()),
     "model_average_predicted_share": float(tier_preds[f"p_{name}"].mean())}
    for i, name in enumerate(TIER_NAMES)
])
tm = {r["tier"]: r for r in tier_mix.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(tier_mix, pct_cols=["share_of_earlier_converters", "share_of_test_converters", "model_average_predicted_share"],
     caption="Expected tier mix: shares among FY1999 to FY2021 and FY2022 to FY2024 converters, and the model's average predicted share")
assert TIER_CHOICE == "most-common-tier rule" and tier_gain["low"] < 0
rule, multi = tt["most-common-tier rule"], tt["multinomial logistic regression"]
assert abs(rule["exact_accuracy"] - tm["$1,200"]["share_of_test_converters"]) < 1e-12   # the rule names $1,200 for everyone
assert auc_low > 0.5 and tier_point["auc"] < 0.7
assert tm["$2,000"]["share_of_test_converters"] > tm["$2,000"]["share_of_earlier_converters"]
ec = {r["cohort"]: r for r in era_check.iter_rows(named=True)}
assert all(ec[t]["predicted_5000_share_kept"] > 0.3 > 0.06 > ec[t]["predicted_5000_share_dropped"] for t in (2023, 2024))
n_by_year = dict(tier_preds.group_by("t").len().iter_rows())
kept_acc = sum(ec[t]["exact_accuracy_kept"] * n_by_year[t] for t in TEST_COHORTS) / sum(n_by_year.values())
"tier claims hold"
'tier claims hold'
  • The tier cannot be predicted better than by naming the most common one. In every training window most converters landed at $1,200 to $1,999, so the rule predicts that tier for everyone and is right 59.0% of the time (50.7% to 67.6%). The regression is right 57.5% of the time, 1.5 points less (-3.8 to 0.0), and names a higher tier for only 1.5% of converters. Under R5 the rule stands.
  • Within one tier is close to automatic. Both approaches are within one tier for 97% of converters, because only the 4 test converters who reached $5,000 or more can be two tiers from a $1,200 prediction.
  • Kate’s two-level indicator carries a weak signal. Ranking converters by the model’s probability of reaching $2,000 or more gives an AUC of 0.63 (0.53 to 0.71). A randomly chosen converter who reached $2,000 outranks one who stopped at $1,200 about 63% of the time, better than a coin flip but far from reliable. It belongs in the dashboard only as a labeled weak signal, as decision D16 set.
  • Recent converters give more. Among the FY1999 to FY2021 converters, 29% reached $2,000 to $4,999; among the FY2022 to FY2024 test converters, 38% did. The regression’s average predicted mix (72% / 23% / 5%) follows the older converters. The mix among recent converters (59% / 38% / 3% for the three tiers) is the better guide for the expected mix shown with the list.

Why soft credits before FY t are left out of these models. The tier models train on converters from FY1999, but soft credits before FY t were recorded only from FY2021. When the input was kept, 8% and 13% of the training converters had it recorded for the FY2023 and FY2024 tests, but every test converter did. The model then extrapolated: its average predicted $5,000+ share rose to 32% and 41%, against observed shares of 0% and 7%, and its exact accuracy over the three test cohorts fell to 39.6%. Without the input, the predicted share is 5% and 6%. We found this after the first run and dropped the input from every model trained from FY1999: the tier models and the 3 and 5 year models. R5’s decision is the same either way, and the 3 and 5 year test scores are unchanged (they differ by at most 3e-14), because the input was missing in every one of their training windows. It matters for the FY2026 scores in the last section, whose training windows reach into FY2021 and later. The 12 month model keeps the input, since there it only marks the FY2021 cohort (see What Drives the Score).

The practical reading is that whether a new major donor gives $1,200 or $2,000 is barely visible in the giving history before conversion. It may depend on things these data do not record, such as the size of the ask or the donor’s relationship with an officer. For the working queue, the tier is best shown as an expected mix, with Kate’s indicator as a weak hint about who might give more.

8 Major Donor Retention

PBS Utah’s major gift officers told us they are most interested in current major donors at risk of dropping off. The group EDA found that more than half of each year’s major donors fall below $1,200 the next year (decision D19). This section ranks current major donors by that risk and reports the dollars exposed. The donor-level touchpoints after a donor becomes major (welcome letters, updates, thank-you cards) are not recorded. So the ranking predicts who is likely to drop, not how much outreach could recover.

The setup mirrors the 12 month model:

  • Who and what. Each row is a major donor at the end of FY t, under the household rule. The outcome is falling below $1,200 in FY t+1.
  • Model. The selected family, an untuned L2 logistic regression, on the giving-history use list without the contact flags, since the cultivation program selected non-major donors.
  • Training window. FY2021 onward, as for the 12 month model (decision D7). Drops were much rarer in the legacy years, so older cohorts would describe a different pattern.
  • Test. A rolling test on FY2022 to FY2024, with FY2025 scored once as a report-only check.
  • Benchmarks. Ranking the lowest givers first, the donors closest to the $1,200 line, is the benchmark in R6. Samantha’s decline-and-recency score (the share of giving lost since the year before, plus years since the last gift) is reported alongside it.
  • The rule (R6). Officers can work only so many major donors closely, so Samantha measured each ranking at capacities of 25 and 50 donors a year. The model is recommended only if its top 25 each year holds more donors who dropped than the lowest-givers-first list, with a paired 95% interval above zero. The top 50 and ROC AUC are reported alongside.
next_year = person_years.select("constituent_id", t=(pl.col("fy") - 1).cast(pl.Int32), next_total="total", next_major="major")
major_fys = person_years.filter(pl.col("major")).select("constituent_id", major_fy=pl.col("fy").cast(pl.Int32))
major_rows = person_years.filter(pl.col("major") & pl.col("fy").is_between(MAIN_START, 2025)).select(
    "constituent_id", "couple_id", t=pl.col("fy").cast(pl.Int32), prior_total="total")
major_rows = major_rows.with_columns(former_major=pl.struct("constituent_id", "t").is_in(
    major_rows.select("constituent_id", "t").join(major_fys, on="constituent_id").filter(pl.col("major_fy") < pl.col("t"))
    .select(pl.struct("constituent_id", "t")).to_series().implode()))
raw_days = bp.giving_features(major_rows, person_years, bp.individual_gifts(clean)).select(
    "constituent_id", "t", raw_days="days_since_last_gift")
retention = (
    build_features(major_rows, clean, person_years)
    .join(next_year, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    .join(raw_days, on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    .with_columns(next_total=pl.col("next_total").fill_null(0.0), next_major=pl.col("next_major").fill_null(False))
    .with_columns(
        y_drop=~pl.col("next_major"),
        decline=pl.max_horizontal(pl.col("prior_total") - pl.col("next_total"), pl.lit(0.0)),
        lowest_first=-pl.col("prior_total"),   # R6 benchmark: the lowest givers among major donors first
        # Samantha's benchmark: share of giving lost since FY t-1, plus years since the last gift
        decline_recency=(pl.when(pl.col("prev_total") > 0)
                         .then(pl.max_horizontal(pl.col("prev_total") - pl.col("prior_total"), pl.lit(0.0)) / pl.col("prev_total"))
                         .otherwise(0.0) + pl.col("raw_days").fill_null(0) / 365))
    .with_columns(y=pl.col("y_drop"), w=pl.lit(1.0))
    .sort("t", "constituent_id")
)
assert retention.select("constituent_id", "t").is_unique().all() and (retention["prior_total"] >= 0).all()
assert not retention["contacted"].any() and not retention["held_out"].any()   # the program selected non-major donors

ret_counts = retention.group_by("t").agg(
    major_donors=pl.len(), dropped=pl.col("y_drop").sum(),
    dropped_but_still_gave=(pl.col("y_drop") & (pl.col("next_total") > 0)).sum(),
    gave_exactly_1200=(pl.col("prior_total") == 1200).sum(),
    giving=pl.col("prior_total").sum(), decline=pl.col("decline").sum()).sort("t")
show(ret_counts.rename({"t": "cohort"}), fixed={"giving": 0, "decline": 0},
     caption="Major donors at each snapshot, how many fell below $1,200 the next year, and the dollars they gave and lost")
RETENTION_FEATURES = [f for f in USE_LIST if f not in TRAINING_ONLY]
RETENTION_SPEC = {**CANDIDATES[SELECTED][0], "name": "major donor retention, untuned L2", "features": RETENTION_FEATURES,
                  "train_start": MAIN_START}
retention_run = cached_nested(RETENTION_SPEC, None, data=retention, target="y_drop")
retention_check = cached_nested(RETENTION_SPEC, None, data=retention, target="y_drop", test_cohorts=[2025])
RET_SCORES = {"model": "model", "lowest giving first": "lowest_first", "decline and recency (Samantha)": "decline_recency"}

def retention_frame(run, cohorts):
    return retention.filter(pl.col("t").is_in(cohorts)).join(run[0].rename({"score": "model"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")

def retention_auc(df, reps=REPS, seed=SEED):
    # ROC AUC for each ranking on couple-clustered resamples, paired across rankings
    couples = df["couple_id"].unique().sort()
    idx = couples.search_sorted(df["couple_id"]).to_numpy()
    y = df["y"].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy()
    s = {k: df[c].cast(pl.Float64).to_numpy() for k, c in RET_SCORES.items()}
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    draws = {k: np.empty(reps) for k in s}
    for r in range(reps):
        mult = np.bincount(rng.integers(0, len(couples), len(couples)), minlength=len(couples))[idx].astype(float)
        for k in s:
            draws[k][r] = roc_auc_score(y, s[k], sample_weight=mult)
    return {k: roc_auc_score(y, s[k]) for k in s}, draws

def exposed(df, col, k):
    # average per year of FY t giving, and of the next year's decline, among the top k by col (ties split evenly)
    d = with_list_share(df, col, "on_list", k)
    years = df["t"].n_unique()
    return float((d["on_list"] * d["prior_total"]).sum() / years), float((d["on_list"] * d["decline"]).sum() / years)

def retention_results(run, cohorts):
    df = retention_frame(run, cohorts)
    assert df["model"].null_count() == 0
    auc_point, auc_draws = retention_auc(df)
    rows, boots = [], {}
    for cap in (25, 50):
        b = boots[cap] = bootstrap(df, RET_SCORES, k=cap)
        for name, col in RET_SCORES.items():
            lo, hi = np.quantile(b["draws"][name][:, 0], [0.025, 0.975])
            d_ = paired(b, name, "lowest giving first") if name != "lowest giving first" else None
            give, lost = exposed(df, col, cap)
            rows.append({"capacity": cap, "ranking": name, "droppers_found": b["point"][name][0] * float(df["y"].sum()),
                         "share_of_droppers": b["point"][name][0], "share_low": lo, "share_high": hi,
                         "precision": b["point"][name][0] * float(df["y"].sum()) / (cap * df["t"].n_unique()),
                         "gain": None if d_ is None else 100 * d_["gain"], "gain_low": None if d_ is None else 100 * d_["low"],
                         "gain_high": None if d_ is None else 100 * d_["high"],
                         "giving_exposed_per_year": give, "decline_per_year": lost})
    auc_rows = []
    for name in RET_SCORES:
        diff = auc_draws[name] - auc_draws["lowest giving first"]
        auc_rows.append({"ranking": name, "auc": auc_point[name], "auc_low": float(np.quantile(auc_draws[name], 0.025)),
                         "auc_high": float(np.quantile(auc_draws[name], 0.975)),
                         "gain_vs_lowest_first": auc_point[name] - auc_point["lowest giving first"],
                         "gain_low": float(np.quantile(diff, 0.025)), "gain_high": float(np.quantile(diff, 0.975))})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows), pl.DataFrame(auc_rows), boots

ret_caps, ret_aucs, ret_boots = retention_results(retention_run, TEST_COHORTS)
r25 = paired(ret_boots[25], "model", "lowest giving first")
RETENTION_RECOMMENDED = r25["low"] > 0   # R6
rc_ = {(r["capacity"], r["ranking"]): r for r in ret_caps.iter_rows(named=True)}
ra_ = {r["ranking"]: r for r in ret_aucs.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(ret_caps, pct_cols=["share_of_droppers", "share_low", "share_high", "precision"],
     fixed={"droppers_found": 1, "gain": 1, "gain_low": 1, "gain_high": 1, "giving_exposed_per_year": 0, "decline_per_year": 0},
     caption="Major donors who dropped below $1,200, found in each year's top 25 and top 50, FY2022 to FY2024; gains in points of the share found, paired against lowest giving first")
show(ret_aucs, digits=3, caption="ROC AUC for ranking major donors by risk of dropping, FY2022 to FY2024, with the paired gain over lowest giving first")
chk_caps, chk_aucs, chk_boots = retention_results(retention_check, [2025])
ck_ = {(r["capacity"], r["ranking"]): r for r in chk_caps.iter_rows(named=True)}
cka = {r["ranking"]: r for r in chk_aucs.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(chk_caps.filter(pl.col("capacity") == 25).join(chk_aucs.select("ranking", "auc"), on="ranking"),
     pct_cols=["share_of_droppers", "share_low", "share_high", "precision"],
     fixed={"droppers_found": 1, "gain": 1, "gain_low": 1, "gain_high": 1, "giving_exposed_per_year": 0, "decline_per_year": 0, "auc": 3},
     caption="FY2025 check, scored once (report only): the top 25 and ROC AUC")
ret_years = ret_counts.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2025))
drop_rate = float(ret_years["dropped"].sum() / ret_years["major_donors"].sum())
still_gave = float(ret_years["dropped_but_still_gave"].sum() / ret_years["dropped"].sum())
at_1200 = float(ret_years["gave_exactly_1200"].sum() / ret_years["major_donors"].sum())
m25, l25, s25 = rc_[(25, "model")], rc_[(25, "lowest giving first")], rc_[(25, "decline and recency (Samantha)")]
m50 = rc_[(50, "model")]
assert RETENTION_RECOMMENDED and r25["low"] < 0.01                  # clears R6, but only just
assert m50["gain_low"] < 0 < m50["gain_high"]                      # no measurable gain at 50
assert ra_["model"]["gain_low"] < 0 < ra_["model"]["gain_high"]    # nor in AUC
assert s25["gain"] < 0 and ra_["decline and recency (Samantha)"]["auc_low"] < 0.5 < ra_["decline and recency (Samantha)"]["auc_high"]
assert m25["decline_per_year"] > l25["decline_per_year"]
c25 = ck_[(25, "model")]
assert c25["gain_low"] > 0 and cka["model"]["gain_low"] > 0
"retention claims hold"
'retention claims hold'
  • Dropping is common. Of the major donors in FY2021 to FY2025, 57% fell below $1,200 the following year, and 76% of those kept giving at a lower level rather than stopping. 54% of major donors gave exactly $1,200, so “lowest giving first” is mostly a tie among them, split evenly.
  • R6 recommends the model, by a narrow margin. In each year’s top 25, the model found 54 of the donors who dropped over the three test cohorts, against 48.1 for lowest giving first. That is 32.0% of droppers against 28.5%, a paired gain of 3.5 points (0.1 to 8.9). About 72% of the donors on the model’s top 25 dropped, against 64% on the benchmark’s.
  • The gain does not extend beyond the top of the list. At 50 donors a year the two rankings find nearly the same droppers (0.5 points, -4.3 to 6.1), and their ROC AUCs are the same (0.59 and 0.59). The model’s advantage is in choosing the first two dozen names, and the interval barely clears zero.
  • The model’s top 25 covers more dollars. It holds about $40,199 of FY t giving a year, against $30,000 for 25 donors at the $1,200 line, and about $25,085 of the next year’s decline, against $14,181. These are dollars exposed to the risk of dropping, not dollars outreach could recover.
  • Samantha’s decline-and-recency score is weaker on the group population. Its AUC is 0.48 (0.42 to 0.54), no better than chance. In her notebook it was the benchmark her ridge model beat. Here, simply ranking the lowest givers first is the harder bar.
  • The FY2025 check, scored once, is stronger. The model’s top 25 held 21 of the 45 donors who dropped after FY2025, a gain of 15.3 points over lowest giving first (5.5 to 25.2), and its AUC was 0.75 against 0.55. As a report-only check it cannot change anything, but it points the same way.

The model meets the rule we set, so a risk list for the FY2026 major donors goes into the last section. The evidence for it is thinner than for the prospect list. The test gain is narrow and only at the top 25, and there are only about 100 major donors a year to learn from. We would present it to PBS Utah as a test: work the top of the list, record the stewardship touchpoints with a holdout group, and measure whether those donors stay major more often.

9 Business Validation and FY2026 Lists

The model beats the benchmark. This section asks what that is worth to PBS Utah and builds what staff would work from. It covers three things:

  • What the list adds, in converters and dollars, on the test cohorts.
  • The FY2026 lists: the immediate-priority list, the long-term nurture list, and the retention risk list (decisions D18, D19, D22).
  • Two safeguards: the saved, reload-tested models (decision D21) and Kate’s coverage audit of who is on the list.

The release is synthetic, and in the test cohorts simulated contact steered conversion toward donors officers selected. So the dollar figures show how the method would be valued on PBS Utah’s records, not money it would raise (decision D14).

9.1 What the List Adds
